*Illa qalilan* is an exception from the half, as if he said: "Stand up, for less than half the night."

Then the option concerns what lies beyond the half, between it and the third.

It is permissible, when you make *nisfahu* a substitute for *qalilan* and explain it by it, that the second *qalilan* means half of the half, which is a quarter, as if it were said: "or reduce from it a little, its half." Some said: it was voluntary, as shown by the option concerning the amount, and by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: *"And from the night, keep vigil with it as a supererogatory prayer for you."*

As 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The worst of travel is *al-haqhaqah* (rushing hard), and the worst of recitation is *al-hadhramah* (speed), until what is recited in its succession resembles a *thaghr al-alas* (a tooth with close-set teeth)."

[I have not seen this from him through the narration of Mansur. Abu 'Ubayd ibn Qutaybah said in *Gharib* that 'Umar said: "The worst recitation is *al-hazramah*." Ibn al-Mubarak related in *al-Zuhd*, through al-Hasan's narration, that "it used to be said: the worst travel is *al-ju'ju'ah*." 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) was asked about the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and she said: "It was not like your recitation. If a listener wished to count his letters, he could have counted them."

*Tartilan* is an emphasis on the obligation of the command to do it, and that it is indispensable for the reciter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 73, verse 6:

And nasha'a min makanihi wa nashaza means he got up from his place. He said:

We rose toward she-camels whose fat the night-journey had melted, and whose skull-bones had pressed together at the crests [Nasha'na: we rose. Al-khawṣ, plural of khawṣā': a she-camel high at the top and large at the bottom. Al-nai: fat. Al-surā: travelling through the night. Al-qamaḥid: plural of qamaḥdawa, the highest bone of the head. He says: we rose toward huge she-camels whose fat the night-journey had melted, and whose head-bones had pressed together, a metaphor for their being trained in travel and accustomed to it.]

And "qiyam al-layl" (standing in the night), with al-nashi'a being a verbal noun from nasha'a when one stands and rises, on the pattern fā'ila like al-'āqiba. What supports this is what is narrated from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: I said to 'Ā'isha: a man stood up at the beginning of the night; would you say of him that he stood "nāshi'a"?

She said: No, al-nāshi'a is only standing after sleep. So al-nāshi'a was interpreted as standing up from the bed, or the worship that arises at night, that is: occurs and rises. It has been said: it is all the hours of the night, because they occur one after another. And it has been said: it is the first hours of it. And it is narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha and would say: Have you not heard the words of Allah, the Exalted: "Indeed, the rising in the night" — this is nāshi'at al-layl — "it is more effective in wiṭā'" — it is specific to it, unlike the nāshi'at al-nahār (the rising of the day), "more conformity": if you mean the soul, its heart agrees with its tongue; or if you mean the standing (qiyam), worship or the hours, the heart of the one standing agrees with his tongue. Or it is more suitable to what is intended of humility (khushu') and sincerity. And from al-Hasan: more agreement between the secret and the public, because the sight of creatures is cut off.

It was read: ashaddu wat'an, with the fatha and the kasra. The meaning: firmer footing and further from slipping. Or heavier and harsher upon the one praying than the prayer of the day, from his saying, peace be upon him: "O Allah, make Your tread heavy upon Mudar" [agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, and it has already been mentioned in al-Anbiya'].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 73, verse 7:

sabhan (ﷻ) — movement and turning about in your affairs and preoccupations, and you will not be free except at night. That is, its fluffing and the spreading out of its parts, due to the scattering of worry and the dispersal of the heart through preoccupations. He imposed on him the standing in prayer at night, then mentioned the wisdom behind what He imposed on him from it: that the night is more conducive to agreement (of heart and tongue) and more intense for recitation, because of the stillness of the man and the lowering of the voice; and that it is more gathering for the heart and more closing for the scattering of worry than the day, because it is the time when cares are dispersed, thoughts are scattered, and one is occupied with the needs of livelihood and the Hereafter. If something of the night has escaped you, then in the day you have free time in which you can make up for it.

And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to His remembrance by night and by day, and be eager for it. The remembrance of God encompasses everything that is a good form of remembrance: glorification (tasbih), declaring His oneness (tahlil), proclaiming His greatness (takbir), extolling Him (tamjid), affirming His unity (tawhid), prayer (salah), recitation of the Qur'an, study of knowledge, and other things with which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would occupy the hours of his night and day. ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾. Abu Nu'aym also narrated it in al-Hilya in the biography of Abu al-Darda, through Sufyan from Khalaf ibn Hawshab, who said: Abu al-Darda said, similar to the version of al-Bayhaqi.]

It has also been said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

When a man knows that his companion is faced with a matter he wishes to have taken care of, or with an enemy whom he desires to avenge himself upon, and he is capable of it and able to do so, he says: "Leave Me with him" — that is, you need not strive to attain your aim and desire [the editor's note: "you need not strive to attain" — perhaps "in attaining"], except that you leave me to deal with him, by entrusting his affair to me and making me sufficient for him, for in Me is what will relieve your mind and clear away your worry. **Tafsir of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 73, verses 17–18:**

*Yawman* is the object (maf'ul bihi), meaning: "How will you guard yourselves (taqqūna anfusakum) on the Day of Resurrection, which belongs to Him, if you remain in disbelief?"

"...and you did not believe and do righteous deeds." It is also permissible for it to be an adverbial of time (zarf), meaning: "How will you have taqwa (God-consciousness) on the Day of Resurrection if you disbelieved in the world?" It is also permissible for it to be governed by *kafartum* under the interpretation of *jahadtum* (you denied), meaning: "How will you be mindful of God and fear Him if you deny the Day of Resurrection and the recompense?" This is because taqwa (God-consciousness) is fear of His punishment.

*Yaj'alu al-wildana shiban* (which makes children grey-haired) is a metaphor for severity. It is said of a severe day: "A day that greys the foreheads of children." The origin of this is that when worries and sorrows accumulate upon a person, grey hair comes upon him quickly. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*"Worry wears down the stout man into thinness, and greys the forelock of the child and makes him old."*

[[Abu al-Tayyib says: worry diminishes the large, stout man and takes away from him little by little. *Nahufa nahafatan* means he became lean, wasting away. So *nahafa* is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), because it corresponds in meaning to the verb. It is also permissible that it is a specification (tamyiz), meaning: great worry diminishes the stout man in respect of the thinness that arises from it. It is also permissible to make it an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) according to the view of those who do not require the agent of the verb and the verbal noun to be identical.

al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 73, verse 20:

﴿Less than two-thirds of the night.﴾ That is, less than them. The word "adnā" (nearer), which means "less," is used figuratively, because when the distance between two things is short, the space between them is small, and when it is great, the space increases.

It is also read: "wa-nisfahu wa-thuluthahu" (and half of it and a third of it) with the accusative case, meaning that you stand for less than two-thirds, and for half and for a third. This matches what was mentioned at the beginning of the surah: the choice between standing for half in its entirety, between standing for less than it, which is a third, and between standing for more than it, which is the nearer of the two-thirds.

It is also read: "wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthihi" (and half of it and a third of it) with the genitive case, meaning: stand for less than two-thirds and for less than half and a third. This matches the choice between half, which is nearer than two-thirds, the third, which is nearer than half, and the quarter, which is nearer than the third; and this is the last possibility.

﴿And a group of those who are with you.﴾ That is, a group of your companions will also stand.

﴿And Allah measures the night and the day.﴾ No one can measure the night and the day, or know the exact measures of their hours, except Allah alone. Placing His name, may He be exalted, as the subject before the predicate "yuqaddiru" (measures) indicates exclusivity in measuring. The meaning is: you cannot measure it.

The pronoun in ﴿you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ refers to the verbal noun of "yuqaddiru." That is, He knows that you cannot correctly keep track of the times, nor can you calculate them through equalizing and balancing, except by taking the broadest margin for precaution. That is hard for you and burdensome for you.

﴿So He has turned to you in forgiveness﴾ is an expression for granting leave to abandon the prescribed standing, like His saying ﴿He has turned to you and pardoned you, so now associate with them﴾ (2:187). The meaning is that He lifted the blame for leaving it from you, just as He lifts blame from one who repents.

Prayer is referred to as "recitation" because it is a part of its pillars, just as it is referred to as standing, bowing, and prostrating. The intended meaning is: pray what is feasible for you, and what is not impossible of the night prayer. This abrogates the first ruling, and both were then abrogated by the five daily prayers.

It has also been said that it refers to the recitation of the Qur'an itself. It was said: one should recite one hundred verses. Whoever recites one hundred verses in a night will not be confronted by the Qur'an. It was also said:

Whoever recites one hundred verses is recorded among the devout (al-qanitin). It was also said: fifty verses.

The wisdom behind the abrogation has been explained: it is the difficulty of standing in prayer for the sick, for those traveling through the land for trade, and for those striving in the way of Allah. It has also been said that Allah placed those striving in His cause and those traveling to earn lawful livelihood on equal footing.

On the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whatever man brings goods to a city of the cities of the Muslims, patiently and seeking reward, and sells them at the price of that day, he will be with Allah among the martyrs." [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it from the transmission of Farqad al-Sabakhi from Ibrahim from Ibn Mas'ud as a statement of his own (mawquf). Farqad is weak. Ibn Mardawayh connected it, mentioning 'Alqama ibn Ibrahim and 'Abdullah, and traced it back to the Prophet as well, adding: then he recited "and others who travel through the land..." (73:20).]]

On the authority of Abdullah ibn Umar: "No death that I die is dearer to me after being killed in the way of Allah than to die between the two sides of a riding saddle, traveling through the land seeking some of Allah's bounty." [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it from the transmission of al-Qasim ibn Abdullah from his father from Nafi' from Ibn Umar. Its chain is weak. Ibn Mu'abbad narrated it in al-Ta'a wal-Ma'siya from Ibn Wahb from Yunus from Ibn Shihab from Nafi' that Umar said: "No death that Allah has created that I die is dearer to me than dying as a striver in the way of Allah..." al-Bayhaqi, in al-Shu'ab in the thirteenth (section), narrated through 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from al-Zuhri from Abdullah, who mentioned Umar or someone else, saying: "Allah created nothing..."]]

﴿And He knows﴾ is a resumed statement, as if answering a question about the reason for the abrogation.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾ means the prescribed prayer; ﴿and give the obligatory zakat﴾. It has also been said that it refers to zakat al-fitr, since there was no zakat in Mecca; it was made obligatory only later. Whoever interprets it as the obligatory zakat considers the end of the surah to be Medinan.

﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ may mean all voluntary charities; or it may mean paying zakat in the best manner: giving out the best wealth and the most beneficial to the poor, observing intention, seeking the face of Allah, and directing it to the deserving; or it may mean every good deed that relates to the self and wealth.

﴿Better﴾ is the second object of "wajada" (to find). It is a separator (fasl), and it is permissible even though it does not come between two definite nouns, because "afʿal" (more, most) resembles a definite noun in refusing the definite article.

Abu al-Sammal read: "huwa khayrun wa-a'zamu ajran" (it is better and greater in reward), with the nominative case, as subject and predicate.

On the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Muzzammil, Allah will remove from him hardship in this world and the next." [[Al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it with their chains to Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him).]]
